newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche no stranger to debacles in recent years.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche no stranger to debacles in recent years.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Bank AG, fined on Wednesday for irregularities at its British funds arm, has weathered a series of debacles in recent years under outgoing chief executive Hilmar Kopper, who retires next month.

The bank's power as a major industrial stakeholder and its relentless expansion into investment banking expose it to regular public criticism and have made it more prone to upsets like the Peter Young affair, analysts say.

British fund industry watchdog IMRO on Wednesday announced Deutsche's London investment bank unit Morgan Grenfell must pay a record two million-pound fine for mismanaging three investment funds and breaching IMRO rules.

Peter Young, who managed two of the funds, was dismissed after the problems came to light last September. The bank also severed ties with four more managers and has reviewed its control and operating methods.

The fine by the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation is negligible compared with the 1.1 to 1.2 billion marks Deutsche set aside in 1996 to cover the cost of the affair, in part to pay compensation.
The bank is no stranger to criticism and Kopper, whose forthright manner has in the past made matters worse, usually appears unfazed by it.

His infamous "peanuts" comment seems destined to be associated with Deutsche long after he steps down to make way for Rolf Breuer, an eloquent investment banker whose smoother style is expected to project a less abrasive image for the bank.
Kopper in 1994 dismissed as "peanuts" millions of marks in unpaid bills owed to tradesmen by tycoon Juergen Schneider, whose property group collapsed under more than five billion marks of debt.

Deutsche was Schneider's biggest single creditor and quickly became the focus of public anger at the ease with which Schneider -- now awaiting trial in a Frankfurt jail on fraud charges -- allegedly duped banks into lending him billions.

In a more recent bout of criticism, 30,000 steelworkers last month demonstrated outside Deutsche's twin-towered headquarters in Frankfurt against its role in backing a hostile takeover bid by steelmaker Krupp AG for rival Thyssen AG.

Deutsche was accused of conducting its own industrial policy and putting jobs at risk for its own financial gain but Kopper rejected the outcry as unfounded and said the bank had only been doing its job.
Back in England, Deutsche hit headlines in January when Morgan Grenfell suspended fund manager Nicola Horlick, accusing her of negotiating to defect to another bank with a team of colleagues.
Horlick responded by flying to Germany in a blaze of media attention to confront Deutsche managers in Frankfurt.

Deutsche is so big -- its total assets exceed those of its closest rival Dresdner Bank AG by more than 300 billion marks -- that it frequently bears the brunt of criticism of perceived excessive bank power and of German banks in general.

Its position as industrial stakeholder cost it dear last year when it contributed about half to a one-billion mark bailout of engineering group KHD, which has since been restructured and renamed Deutz. The bank owns more than 25 percent of Deutz.
In 1993, it was involved in the rescue of Metallgesellschaft AG which came close to bankruptcy due to losses on risky oil contracts trading in the U.S.
